title: Author Correction: Advanced glycation end-products as mediators of the aberrant crosslinking of extracellular matrix in scarred liver tissue

summary: Healthy articular cartilage maintains ultralow friction through the lipid/hyaluronic acid/lubricin complex lubrication layer, in which the zwitterionic lipids mediate lubrication and the hyaluronic acid and lubricin anchor to cartilage matrix. However, in osteoarthritis this lubrication system is progressively degraded, leading to increased cartilage wear and joint dysfunction. Therefore, early and lubrication-based intervention is urgently needed. Here we present biomimetic polyzwitterionic coacervates (pZCOs) that recapitulate both the lubrication and cartilage-binding functionalities of the natural boundary lubrication layer. pZCOs exhibit strong binding affinity to fibronectin, establish a stable and ultralow-friction lubrication layer on the cartilage surface, facilitate the sustained release of anti-inflammatory drugs, and preserve the viability and anti-inflammatory paracrine secretion of encapsulated mesenchymal stem cells. In both rat and mini-pig models of osteoarthritis, intra-articular administration of drug/MSC-laden pZCOs effectively reduces cartilage degradation, suppresses inflammation and promotes cartilage integrity, outperforming clinical hyaluronic acid lubricants in lubrication performance, in vivo retention and therapeutic efficacy. These findings highlight the translational potential of engineered biomimetic coacervates as next-generation joint lubricants for integrated management of osteoarthritis. Polyzwitterionic coacervates with therapeutic payload delivery, mimicking physiological lubrication and cartilage-binding functionalities, reduce joint friction and inflammation in rat and mini-pig osteoarthritis models.
title: Cartilage-binding coacervate with therapeutic payload delivery and biomimetic lubrication alleviates osteoarthritis by reducing joint friction and inflammation

title: Red blood cell-derived extracellular vesicles as a potent autologous adjuvant

summary: Local activation of regulatory T (Treg) cells represents a promising strategy for wound repair and tissue regeneration. However, current Treg-based therapies rely on adoptive cell transfer, which requires ex vivo expansion and reinfusion, posing challenges to donor variability and tissue specificity. Here we engineer a hydrogel-based system for in situ Treg activation at injury sites through the controlled release of AS2863619 (AS), a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor. AS is incorporated into collagen hydrogels at concentrations exceeding its solubility limit, reducing burst release and extending the release half-life. This continuous exposure to Treg-inducing agents stabilizes Foxp3 expression in CD4+ T cells, thereby enabling Treg induction and stabilization. The incorporation of laponite nanoparticles further slows AS release and prolongs drug retention. In a calvarial bone-defect model, AS-loaded hydrogels induce dose-dependent Treg cell activation, reduce pro-inflammatory macrophage responses and enhance bone regeneration. Notably, AS–laponite hydrogels achieve complete defect bridging in some cases. By providing spatiotemporal control over Treg populations without the need for cell isolation and expansion, this approach offers a scalable alternative for immunomodulation and tissue repair. A laponite nanoparticles-based hydrogel loaded with a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor induces localized regulatory T (Treg) cell activation directly in vivo and enhances bone regeneration in a calvarial bone-defect mouse model.
title: Hydrogel for sustained and localized delivery of a regulatory T cell-inducing agent promotes bone regeneration

summary: Improving outcomes for high-risk acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) patients requires increasingly personalized treatment strategies that leverage molecular and omics-based assays as well as functional screens. However, to date, only a few of these approaches are clinically actionable and easily adopted in clinical settings. To that end, we report a combination drug screening assay (GradientScreen) that correlates with clinical outcomes using standard paediatric ALL treatment protocols. This assay uses a microfluidic device to generate overlapping drug gradients and implements an analysis framework that characterizes drug synergy and efficacy in a ratiometric manner. Using partial least squares regression, we show that our combination response metrics correlate with both minimal residual disease (MRD) following initiation of treatment and later clinical end-points. Here, we further demonstrate that this system could be used to evaluate response to experimental therapeutic regimens in patients who did not respond to standard treatment. This assay can serve as a research-enabling tool for the field, with potential to integrate into clinical pathology workflows to identify difficult-to-treat ALL patients and screen for alternative treatment strategies at diagnosis. A gradient-based microfluidic framework analyses the functional responses of leukaemia cells from paediatric ALL patients to ratiometric combinations of three candidate drugs.
title: Gradient-driven microfluidic framework for the screening of ratiometric drug combinations towards precision oncology in paediatric leukaemia

summary: Current vaccine adjuvants, such as aluminum salts and emulsions, are limited by weak induction of cytotoxic T cell immunity and restricted ability to promote T helper type 1 responses, highlighting the need for safer and more effective alternatives. Here we show that microparticles generated from erythrocytes by controlled ultraviolet irradiation function as potent T helper type 1-skewing adjuvants that enhance tumour antigen-specific cytotoxic T cell responses in vitro and in multiple mouse tumour models. Following uptake by dendritic cells, these microparticles traffic to lysosomes and deliver haem cargo that is subsequently transported to the nucleus. Mechanistically, the particles elevate lysosomal pH, promoting lysosome movement towards the nucleus and enabling haem transfer, where haem activates REV-ERB⍺ and forms a co-repressor complex that suppresses peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma, thereby relieving inhibition of dendritic cell maturation and antigen presentation. In vaccination settings, combining tumour antigens with erythrocyte-derived microparticles enhances cytotoxic T cell activation and suppresses tumour growth with minimal toxicity. These findings establish host-derived vesicles as a promising platform for next-generation cancer vaccine adjuvants. Microparticles generated from erythrocytes by controlled ultraviolet irradiation act as T helper type 1-skewing adjuvants that enhance tumour antigen-specific cytotoxic T cell responses in vitro and across mouse tumour models.
title: Autologous erythrocyte microparticles drive antitumour T cell immunity via haem-mediated dendritic cell activation

summary: An interpretable neural network, SPACER, learns the rules of cellular recruitment directly from tissue spatial transcriptomics data. Analyses of multiple cancers reveal a role for the local antigen presentation machinery and tumour mucins in T cell recruitment to tumours, and a mouse model of severe checkpoint inhibitor-induced myocarditis identifies CD4+ T cells as key disease effectors.
title: An interpretable AI model decodes the rules of cell recruitment to specific destinations
